accroche: The “noble savage” attributed to Rousseau appears in none of his texts. The myth is far older than he is.
contenu_vulgarise:
Jean-Jacques Rousseau is almost systematically credited with the idea of the “noble savage” (in French, “bon sauvage”): man, naturally innocent and happy, whom civilization would corrupt. The expression itself, however, appears nowhere in his work. Rousseau never wrote it.

## An earlier myth, a methodological hypothesis

The myth existed well before him. As early as the 15th and 16th centuries, the accounts of the first explorers (Christopher Columbus, Amerigo Vespucci) already describe the newly encountered peoples in terms that oscillate between contempt and fascination. It is above all Montaigne, in his essay “Des coches” (“Of Coaches”) in the late 16th century, who lays the foundations of the contrast: he sets the rationality he attributes to the peoples of the New World against the violence of the European conquerors, a critique of Europe disguised as praise of elsewhere.

What Rousseau actually writes, in the *Discours sur l'origine et les fondements de l'inégalité parmi les hommes* (*Discourse on the Origin and Foundations of Inequality Among Men*, 1755), is more cautious than people think. He describes there a purely hypothetical state of nature (“a condition which no longer exists, which perhaps did not exist, which probably never will exist,” he writes in the preface) in which men would have lived “free, healthy, good, and happy lives, as much as their nature enabled them to do so.” It is a thought experiment meant to isolate what life in society adds to man, not a historical account of real peoples observed in the field.

His contemporaries, for their part, are not entirely fooled, or choose to be. Voltaire, on receiving the *Discours*, replies to Rousseau on August 30, 1755, with a famous letter: “No one has ever been so witty as you are in trying to turn us into brutes: to read your book makes one long to go on all fours.” The line caricatures a thesis more nuanced than the attack suggests. And it is this caricature, more than Rousseau's text itself, that ended up shaping the image of the philosopher nostalgic for a primitive paradise.

## What this shifts

The misreading is not just an error of attribution. It makes a single author carry an imaginary (that of the virtuous “savage,” an inverted mirror of our own faults) that runs through five centuries of European literature and that says, most of the time, more about the Europe that formulated it than about the societies it claimed to describe. Rousseau merely inherited, late in the day, an image that he neither invented nor, to the letter, ever endorsed.

carte.idee: The expression systematically attributed to Rousseau appears in none of his texts. The myth predates him by two centuries, and it is above all Voltaire's caricature of it that fixed his image as the philosopher of the noble savage.

pour_aller_plus_loin.note: Overview of the history of the expression and its uses.

quiz.question: What does Voltaire reply when he discovers Rousseau's Discourse on Inequality?
choix: He unreservedly praises the description of a lost paradise
He says he is convinced of the usefulness of returning to the state of nature
He loftily ignores the text and never replies
He mocks the thesis by mentioning the urge to walk on all fours
quiz.explication: In his letter of August 30, 1755, Voltaire ironically mocks Rousseau's thesis by writing that his book makes one “long to go on all fours,” proof that the caricature of the philosopher nostalgic for the savage state dates from Rousseau's own time.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Who, before Rousseau, sets out in the late 16th century the contrast between the rationality attributed to the peoples of the New World and the violence of the European conquerors?
quiz_supplementaire.explication: It is Montaigne who, in the essay Des coches (“Of Coaches”) in the late 16th century, sets out this contrast: a critique of Europe disguised as praise of elsewhere, well before Rousseau.

quiz_supplementaire.question: How does Rousseau present, in the preface to the 1755 Discourse, the state of nature he describes?
choix: As a historical state, attested by the explorers' accounts
As a hypothetical state, which perhaps never existed
As the state of the peoples he himself observed on his travels
As a state still observable in his lifetime, in certain regions
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Rousseau writes from the preface onward that it is a condition that no longer exists, that perhaps did not exist, and that probably never will exist: a thought experiment, not a historical account.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What does the entry say the myth of the noble savage ultimately reveals?
choix: It mainly reveals Rousseau's personal intentions toward his mentor
It reveals nothing, being a pure invention with no relation to reality
It reveals more about the societies observed than about the Europe that formulated it
It reveals more about the Europe that formulated it than about the societies it claimed to describe
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The misreading makes a single author carry an imaginary that says, most of the time, more about the Europe that formulated it than about the societies it claimed to describe.
